summary: Elliot Brandt is the chief executive officer of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, succeeding Howard Kohr at the end of 2024 after decades of regional advocacy, donor mobilization and senior leadership. Under an electoral strategy introduced in 2021, AIPAC operates a federal PAC and the United Democracy Project super PAC, while Brandt has personally advocated continued, largely unconditional U.S. military assistance to Israel. In October 2026 he co-signed a strategic shift away from formal endorsements and direct PAC contributions, while retaining the super PAC and pursuing organized individual giving.

chapters.title: Origins and recruitment into AIPAC
chapters.dek: Elliot Brandt is the chief executive officer of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, succeeding Howard Kohr at the end of 2024 after decades of regional advocacy, donor mobilization and senior leadership. Under an electoral strategy introduced in 2021, AIPAC operates a federal PAC and the United Democracy Project super PAC, while Brandt has personally advocated continued, largely unconditional U.S. military assistance to Israel. In October 2026 he co-signed a strategic shift away from formal endorsements and direct PAC contributions, while retaining the super PAC and pursuing organized individual giving.
chapters.body:
Brandt emerged from political and Jewish communal work rather than an electoral office. An official biography submitted to a House committee says that he worked on medical-supply logistics serving the former Soviet Union and completed an Otzma fellowship year in Israel before joining AIPAC in its Pacific Northwest office in 1994. An independent 2024 profile gives his Stanford graduation year as 1990. His birth date and exact early professional chronology remain unverified. [[EB01, EB03]]

The official biography is a useful primary source for institutional resume data, but it is not an independent assessment of success or influence. Keep unverified personal details out of the production record. [[EB01, EB03]]

chapters.title: Regional politics: 13 states and more than 100 districts
chapters.body:
In 2002 Brandt became Western States director in Los Angeles, with responsibility for political and coalition work across 13 states and more than 100 congressional districts, according to his congressional biography. A 2003 Jewish Journal interview supplies contemporaneous context for his move from Northern to Southern California. [[EB01, EB05, EB06]]

This decade mattered as a training ground for donor relationships and district-level mobilization, although the precise funding network and role in individual candidate decisions cannot be established from a job title. Jewish Insider reported that Brandt moved to Washington as managing director in 2015. [[EB01, EB05, EB06]]

chapters.title: From lobbying to electoral machinery
chapters.body:
AIPAC long concentrated on constituent advocacy and lawmaker relationships, while its name used PAC to mean Public Affairs Committee rather than an FEC political action committee. In December 2021 it launched an actual PAC (FEC C00797670) and announced a super PAC, which registered as United Democracy Project in January 2022 (FEC C00799031). [[EB09, EB10, EB11, EB02, EB12]]

These are legally and financially distinct channels. Traditional PAC donations and individual earmarks entering campaigns differ from UDP independent expenditures, which may be unlimited but legally cannot coordinate with candidates. AIPAC itself credited Brandt with a key role in the expansion, but no public record in this research proves he personally ordered a particular ad buy. [[EB09, EB10, EB11, EB02, EB12]]

chapters.title: 2024 CEO succession and institutional governance
chapters.body:
The AIPAC board announced in June 2024 that Brandt would succeed Howard Kohr at the end of the year. He had become vice CEO in January and previously managed national affairs. AIPAC credited him with expanding donor engagement and said organizational and political fundraising doubled under his leadership; these are organizational assessments, not a proven estimate of the money personally raised by Brandt. [[EB02, EB06, EB08, EB19]]

Current organizational material says the board sets strategic political and policy directives while the CEO leads staff. The October 2026 signed letter places Brandt among an identifiable leadership group, including President Bernie Kaminetsky, Chair Michael Tuchin and President-elect Yehuda Neuberger. [[EB02, EB06, EB08, EB19]]

chapters.title: The congressional funding agenda
chapters.body:
Brandt submitted written testimony to a House Appropriations subcommittee on April 2, 2025, calling for $3.3 billion in FY2026 Israeli security assistance. He argued for an American strategic and industrial benefit from the alliance and opposed attaching further political conditions to Israeli security assistance and arms sales. [[EB07]]

The testimony is firsthand evidence of what Brandt advocated, not objective proof that every security claim is correct. It also supported U.S. aid for Egypt and Jordan, a Middle East peace partnership program and Israeli-Palestinian security coordination subject to conditions. [[EB07]]

chapters.title: Electoral leverage: victories, reversals and attribution
chapters.body:
In 2024 UDP spent heavily against Jamaal Bowman and for George Latimer in New York, and opposed Cori Bush in Missouri. Documented spending and results belong in linked committee/candidate records, not written as direct payments from Brandt. A 2026 FactCheck review also documents UDP spending in several primaries, including opposition to Republican Thomas Massie. [[EB12, EB13, EB14, EB15, EB16, EB18]]

The Michigan Senate Democratic primary is a counterexample to claims of automatic dominance: a transaction-deduplicated analysis found UDP spent $30.64 million supporting Haley Stevens or opposing Abdul El-Sayed, yet El-Sayed won. Critics say overt primary interventions alienate Democratic allies, while AIPAC argues it must defend pro-Israel lawmakers; neither narrative alone establishes causal election effects. [[EB12, EB13, EB14, EB15, EB16, EB18]]

chapters.title: Donors, affiliates and careful financial accounting
chapters.body:
AIPAC PAC and UDP have distinct federal filings. For reports covering Jan 2025 through Oct 14, 2026, the FEC lists $57.77 million in AIPAC PAC receipts and $112.82 million in UDP receipts. UDP reported $85.06 million in total disbursements and $53.60 million in independent expenditures in regular summary records. Those figures must not be summed as though they represent distinct final spending or as donations received by candidates. [[EB10, EB11, EB12, EB17, EB26, EB27]]

AIPAC’s nonprofit Form 990 reports $122.54 million in FY2025 revenue and $118.29 million in expenses, a separate fiscal year and reporting universe. Its executive disclosure gives Brandt $862,888 reportable compensation from the organization and $46,447 other compensation. Large UDP donors named in independent FEC work include Paul Singer and Haim Saban; a transaction is not proof of a personal relationship or improper coordination. [[EB10, EB11, EB12, EB17, EB26, EB27]]

chapters.title: Israel, Iran and the limits of organizational attribution
chapters.body:
In his 2025 testimony, Brandt publicly argued that unconditional security aid and technological cooperation with Israel served U.S. interests. In 2026 AIPAC issued organizational statements supporting American-Israeli military operations against Iran and demanding robust restrictions in any diplomatic arrangement. An AIPAC memo also promoted U.S.–Israel defense technology provisions in the proposed FY2027 authorization bill. [[EB07, EB22, EB23, EB24, EB25]]

The policy apparatus he leads supported these positions, but the public releases are corporate statements rather than verified personal quotations by Brandt. Present AIPAC’s substantive arguments and relevant criticism of aid conditionality without presenting either as established fact. [[EB07, EB22, EB23, EB24, EB25]]

chapters.title: Backlash: the costs of public electioneering
chapters.body:
Independent reporting in October 2026 described prominent donor cultivation and closely coordinated strategic leadership between Brandt and UDP head Rob Bassin, while some longstanding supporters criticized AIPAC for endorsing election-denying Republicans, polarizing primaries and weakening its bipartisan image. AIPAC defended the strategy as essential to supporting politicians aligned with the U.S.–Israel alliance. [[EB18, EB12, EB27]]

Criticism of political spending is not itself proof of illegal lobbying, prohibited coordination, or foreign direction. Conversely, AIPAC’s assurances are organizational advocacy and should not be taken as independent audits of influence or compliance. [[EB18, EB12, EB27]]

chapters.title: October 2026 strategic reversal
chapters.body:
On October 21, AIPAC informed members that it would end candidate endorsements, direct PAC contributions and earmarking, while sustaining the UDP super PAC and increasing organized individual candidate donations. The membership letter was signed by Brandt and fellow leadership officials. The precise effective date for each promised withdrawal is not established in the excerpts reviewed. [[EB19, EB20, EB21]]

The announcement is a major strategic change, but not a withdrawal from election activity. It is especially consequential for longitudinal political-money dashboards: pre-change AIPAC PAC conduit/earmark records must not be projected mechanically into 2028, and post-change outside spending or member-directed donations must be tracked on their separate legal records. [[EB19, EB20, EB21]]
